passage: Class teacher's note, Class 5. Amandeep and Jeevan have been inseparable since Class 1. This week a new boy, Farhan, joined and sits next to Jeevan in maths. Today at lunch Amandeep sat at the far end of the bench, not eating. When Jeevan laughed at something Farhan said, Amandeep said loudly, "He's only nice to you because you have the new bat." Later he tore a page in his notebook and said it was an accident. I spoke with him quietly. He said, "Jeevan will forget me." I have paired all three for next week's science model.

qa.q: Where does Farhan sit in maths?
qa.a: He sits next to Jeevan.

qa.q: What was Amandeep afraid of, based on what he told the teacher?
qa.a: That Jeevan would forget him and choose the new boy as his friend instead.

qa.q: Why is pairing all three for the science model a sensible step?
qa.a: It lets Amandeep see he can share Jeevan without losing him, and gives him a chance to know Farhan.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel hearing "He's only nice to you because you have the new bat"?
qa.a: Hurt and unwelcome, since he is new and the remark says his friendship isn't real.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a boy's fear of losing his best friend to a newcomer.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Ma'am gave the Annual Day solo to the new girl, Kirti. I've sung the solo for three years. Everyone clapped for her at practice, even Mridul, who always says my voice is the best. I clapped too, but my hands felt stiff. At lunch Mridul sat with her to ask how she learned. I stayed in the classroom pretending to finish homework. What if everyone likes her more now? What if Mridul does? I know Kirti didn't do anything wrong. That makes it worse, somehow. 😔
- Himani

qa.q: What did Ma'am give to Kirti?
qa.a: The Annual Day solo.

qa.q: What was Himani afraid of when Mridul sat with Kirti?
qa.a: Himani feared losing the spot as the best singer and losing Mridul's attention to the new girl.

qa.q: What small step could help Himani with this feeling?
qa.a: Talking to Mridul or a trusted adult about the feeling, and perhaps asking Ma'am about another part to sing.

qa.q: How might Kirti experience the class?
qa.a: As a new girl she may simply feel relieved to be welcomed, unaware that Himani is hurting.

grounding: It shows a child afraid of losing both her status as the singer and a friend's attention to a new rival.

passage: In the village, Sahil and Vijay had grazed the goats together every evening since they were small. Then Kamlesh's cousin came from the city for the summer with a real leather football, and Vijay started going to the school ground instead. On the third evening, Sahil walked the goats alone past the ground. He could hear Vijay shouting, "Pass! Pass!" Sahil didn't look. He whacked a bush with his stick harder than he needed to. At home he told his mother the goats were slow today, and he went to bed without eating his rotis.

qa.q: What did the city cousin bring?
qa.a: A real leather football.

qa.q: Why did Sahil whack the bush harder than he needed to?
qa.a: He was hurt that Vijay was choosing the city boy's game over their evenings together, and the feeling came out through his arm.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil to do?
qa.a: Tell Vijay he misses their evenings, or go to the ground and ask to join, instead of staying away alone.

qa.q: What might Vijay not realise about Sahil?
qa.a: He may be enjoying the new football and not notice that Sahil feels left behind.

grounding: It shows a village boy's fear of losing his friend to a newcomer with something exciting to offer.

passage: When Sunaina rode into the kasba square on a new red bicycle with a bell and a basket, every child ran to look. Jagdish, ten, stood at the back. His own cycle was his uncle's old one, too tall, with a chain that fell off every week. He watched Sunaina ring the bell twice. He wanted that bell so much his chest hurt. When she asked, "Want to try?" he said, "No, it's a girls' cycle," and walked off. At home he scrubbed his old cycle's rusty handle for an hour, then kicked the tyre.

qa.q: What was wrong with Jagdish's own cycle?
qa.a: It was his uncle's old one, too tall, with a chain that fell off every week.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish say "No, it's a girls' cycle"?
qa.a: He wanted the bicycle so badly that he turned down the offer with an excuse rather than show how much he wished it were his.

qa.q: What could help Jagdish handle this feeling?
qa.a: Admitting to himself or someone he trusts that he wishes he had a cycle like hers, and perhaps accepting the ride next time.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when he walked off?
qa.a: Confused or a bit hurt, since she had offered to share.

grounding: It shows a boy's longing for a peer's new bicycle and how that envy shapes his reaction.

passage: In their school in Toronto, Valentina seemed to glide. She told jokes that made the whole table laugh, and teachers always picked her to read aloud. Abebe, eleven, had arrived from Addis Ababa last year and still thought each sentence through before he said it. At recess he watched her talk to three groups in five minutes. He wished he could just open his mouth like that. That night he practised a joke in the mirror, but it sounded stiff. He thought about his old school, where he had been the one telling stories.

qa.q: Where did Abebe move from?
qa.a: From Addis Ababa, last year.

qa.q: What did Abebe wish as he watched Valentina at recess?
qa.a: He wished he could talk as easily and confidently as she did, without thinking each sentence through.

qa.q: What small step might help Abebe?
qa.a: Share stories with one friend or a small group first, where he feels at ease, instead of copying Valentina's style.

qa.q: What would change if Abebe knew Valentina sometimes felt nervous too?
qa.a: He might envy her less and see that confidence looks easier from the outside.

grounding: It shows a boy wishing for a classmate's easy confidence and social standing, while missing his old self.

passage: At the hostel in Darjeeling, parcels came on Saturdays. Dolma got one almost every week: sweets, a new sweater, a letter with drawings from her little sister. Francis, twelve, had got two parcels all term. He sat on his bed while the others crowded round Dolma's box. She held out a sweet to him. He took it and said, "Thanks," but it tasted too sugary. He wanted a box with his name on it, and letters every week like hers. He turned toward the wall and reread his last letter, soft from folding.

qa.q: On which day did parcels come at the hostel?
qa.a: Parcels came on Saturdays.

qa.q: Why did the sweet taste too sugary to Francis?
qa.a: His envy of Dolma's regular parcels and letters spoiled it; he wanted what she had, not just a sweet.

qa.q: How could a hostel warden help children like Francis on parcel day?
qa.a: Notice who rarely gets parcels and plan a shared treat or letter-writing time, so no one feels left out.

qa.q: How might Dolma see the moment?
qa.a: She was being generous by offering a sweet and probably has no idea how Francis feels.

grounding: It shows a hostel boy envying a peer's parcels and letters from home.

passage: Coach's note, Lalit, under-12 kho-kho. Gopika joined in June and for weeks stood alone at the edge while the girls stretched in a circle. Today, after she tagged out two runners in the final, the team lifted her onto their shoulders. Afterwards the captain tied the team's orange ribbon on her wrist. Gopika touched it all through the bus ride home and kept laughing at nothing. She told me, "Now I'm really in the team." I will keep an eye out that the quieter girls feel part of it too.

qa.q: What did the captain tie on Gopika's wrist?
qa.a: The team's orange ribbon.

qa.q: What does Gopika touching the ribbon all the way home suggest?
qa.a: She felt safe and happy at last to be accepted, and the ribbon was proof she belonged. 🧡

qa.q: Why is Lalit's plan to watch the quieter girls wise?
qa.a: Belonging matters deeply at this age, so making sure no one stays at the edge keeps the whole team secure.

qa.q: What was the team's experience of lifting Gopika?
qa.a: They were celebrating her tags and, maybe without planning it, showing her she was fully one of them.

grounding: It shows, in a coach's note, a girl's deep security and joy once her team accepts her.

passage:
Diary, Friday.
Today Alka said, "Yogesh, you're coming to the science club picnic, na? We kept a spot for you." They'd even written my name on the list with a star. For months I've eaten lunch alone watching their table. Today I sat in the middle. Everyone laughed at my bad joke about the frog. Nobody asked why I talk funny. I wasn't nervous once. I think this is what my cousins mean when they say "our gang." Walking home, I felt like I could carry a whole sack of cement. 😊

qa.q: What did the group put next to Yogesh's name on the list?
qa.a: They put a star next to his name.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel sitting in the middle of the table?
qa.a: Relaxed and secure, not nervous at all, because the group had made room for him and laughed with him.

qa.q: How could Yogesh make this belonging last and pass it on?
qa.a: Keep showing up to the club, and later save a spot for someone else who eats alone.

qa.q: What might Alka have noticed that led her to invite Yogesh?
qa.a: Perhaps that he had been eating alone for months, so keeping him a spot was her way of welcoming him.

grounding: It shows a boy's strong sense of security and worth after a peer group finally includes him.

passage: Every autumn the boys of the para built their own small pandal behind the pond, and Anirban had always watched from his grandmother's veranda. This year Hemant, who ran the group, shouted up, "Anirban! Can you paint? Come!" He ran down so fast he left his slippers behind. They gave him the lion's mane to paint. By evening his hands were yellow, and the other boys were calling him "Lion-babu." On the way home he kept looking back at the lit pandal. That night he told his grandmother, "Next year, they said I can do the eyes."

qa.q: Which part did the boys give Anirban to paint?
qa.a: The lion's mane.

qa.q: What does Anirban running down without his slippers show?
qa.a: He had longed to be part of the group for years and was thrilled to be invited in.

qa.q: How could Hemant help other watching children feel welcome too?
qa.a: Keep calling out to children on the edge and give each one a real job, the way he did with Anirban.

qa.q: How might Anirban's grandmother see the change in him?
qa.a: She may be happy to see him glowing after years of watching from the veranda.

grounding: It shows a small-town boy's joy and security when a peer group takes him in and gives him a nickname.

passage:
Diary, 14th.
Maths test back. I got 11 out of 25. Abhinav got 25, again. He said he didn't even study. Ma'am read out the top marks, and I turned my paper face down fast. Everyone in my row seems to understand fractions except me. Even my handwriting looks messy next to theirs. At home Mummy asked about the test and I said, "Everyone did better than me. I'm just not a maths person." She said, "You're good at other things, Nirmala. My clever girl." I don't feel good at anything tonight. Maybe I'll ask Didi to show me the fraction ones tomorrow.

qa.q: What mark did Nirmala get?
qa.a: She got 11 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala turn her paper face down fast?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and behind when the top marks were read out and didn't want anyone to see hers.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do next, and why is that a good step?
qa.a: Ask Didi for help with fractions, as she plans, because it tackles the actual gap instead of the comparison.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt hearing "I'm just not a maths person"?
qa.a: Worried that one test had shaken Nirmala's view of herself, which is why she pointed to her other strengths.

grounding: It shows a girl feeling inferior after comparing her marks and abilities with a classmate's.

passage: Every evening the village children jumped off the rocks into the river, and Ganga, nine like him, swam across and back twice. Thomas couldn't swim. He sat on the bank with his knees pulled up, pretending to watch the fishermen. When a boy called, "Thomas, come in!" he said his stomach hurt. Ganga shouted, "It's easy!" To her it was. He watched her strong arms and felt small and slow, as if everyone had learned something while he wasn't looking. Walking home, he kicked stones and didn't answer when his father asked about his day.

qa.q: How many times did Ganga swim across and back?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did Thomas say his stomach hurt?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of not being able to swim and wanted an excuse so the others wouldn't find out.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas's father to do?
qa.a: Gently ask about his day again later and, if Thomas shares, offer to teach him or find someone safe to teach him swimming.

qa.q: Why might Ganga's "It's easy!" land badly on Thomas?
qa.a: She meant to encourage him, but because it is easy for her, it made him feel even further behind.

grounding: It shows a village boy feeling small and behind when he compares himself with peers who can swim.

passage: At the athletics trials in Johannesburg, Lindiwe, twelve, ran the 200 metres in her school shoes because her trainers had split. She came fifth. Paulo, who had won every race since Grade 4, finished first without even looking tired, and his parents cheered from the stands. Lindiwe sat on the grass and pulled at her laces. Everyone else seemed to have proper kit, parents watching and a coach's nod. She told herself she would probably never be a real runner. Then Paulo flopped down beside her and said, "Your start was really fast."

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe run in her school shoes?
qa.a: Her trainers had split.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe believe about herself as she pulled at her laces?
qa.a: That she would probably never be a real runner, because everyone else seemed better equipped and better supported.

qa.q: How could a coach respond to Lindiwe after this race?
qa.a: Point out what she did well, like her fast start, and help her find proper shoes through the school if possible.

qa.q: How does Paulo see Lindiwe's race?
qa.a: He noticed her fast start and seems to see her as a real runner, unlike how she sees herself.

grounding: It shows a girl feeling inferior after comparing her kit, support and results with a star runner's.

passage: On the dusty patch behind the panchayat office, Lokesh and three other boys were playing marbles. Ujjwal, the oldest, nudged his marble closer to the hole with his toe when he thought nobody saw. Lokesh saw. His face went hot. "You moved it! I saw your foot!" "I didn't." "You did! That's cheating!" Lokesh's voice cracked, and he stamped so hard the dust flew up. The smaller boys looked from one to the other. Lokesh scooped up his own marbles. "I'm not playing if we don't play fair." He stood there, breathing fast, until Ujjwal kicked the marble back.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal move his marble?
qa.a: He nudged it closer to the hole with his toe.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's cracking voice and stamping suggest?
qa.a: He felt a burst of anger at the unfairness, strong enough to shake his voice.

qa.q: Which part of Lokesh's reaction helped, and what could be calmer?
qa.a: Refusing to play unless it was fair worked; saying it in a steadier voice could keep the fight from growing.

qa.q: How might the smaller boys have seen the argument?
qa.a: They may have been nervous to take sides against the oldest boy, but relieved when someone stood up for fair play.

grounding: It shows a boy's hot reaction to seeing a peer cheat in a game.

passage: In the lunch queue at their school in Manchester, two older boys slid in front of Sofia, laughing. The dinner lady didn't see. Kwame, eleven, felt heat climb up his neck. "Oi, that's not fair, she's been waiting!" he said, louder than he meant. The boys shrugged. "So?" Kwame's fists curled. "So go to the back like everyone else." Sofia tugged his sleeve. "Leave it." But Kwame stepped out of line and told the dinner lady, pointing. When the boys were sent to the back, his hands were still shaking.

qa.q: Where did the older boys push in?
qa.a: In front of Sofia in the lunch queue.

qa.q: Why were Kwame's hands still shaking after the boys were sent back?
qa.a: His anger at the unfairness was still running through him even after things were put right.

qa.q: What went well, and what could Kwame watch out for?
qa.a: Telling the dinner lady fixed it without a fight; he could notice his curled fists so the heat doesn't turn into shoving.

qa.q: Why might Sofia have said "Leave it"?
qa.a: She may have wanted to avoid trouble or attention, even though the unfairness was done to her.

grounding: It shows a boy's heated reaction to queue-jumping and rule-breaking against a classmate.

passage: At the swimming club's Sunday race, Nitin dived a moment before the whistle. People in the stands saw it, but the official didn't call him back, and he won by a hand. Elizabeth, eleven, came second. She climbed out and slapped the water off her arms. "He went early! Everyone saw!" Her cheeks were red, and she wouldn't step onto the podium. "It's not about losing. Rules are rules." The coach put a towel round her. "I'll speak to the official." Elizabeth sat on the bench, jaw tight, still watching Nitin grin with his medal.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth finish in the race?
qa.a: She came second.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth refusing the podium show?
qa.a: She was burning with anger at the early start and didn't want to accept a result she saw as unfair.

qa.q: What would you advise Elizabeth to do next?
qa.a: Let the coach raise it with the official and perhaps take her podium place, since the complaint can go through the proper channel.

qa.q: How might Nitin see things differently?
qa.a: He may not realise he went early, or may not want to admit it, and sees only his win.

grounding: It shows a girl's heated sense of injustice when a rival breaks the start rule and wins.

passage: Last winter my mother was in hospital for a week, and nobody at home remembered my tiffin. On the first day I sat at lunch pretending I wasn't hungry. Chaitanya noticed. He didn't say anything, just tore his paratha in half and slid it over. The next day he brought two parathas. He did it all week and never told anyone. I only found out later that he'd asked his mother to make extra. I still don't know how to repay that. When I thanked him, he just said, "You'd do it too, Nitin." I hope I would.

qa.q: How long did Chaitanya bring extra food?
qa.a: All week.

qa.q: What does Nitin's "I still don't know how to repay that" show?
qa.a: Nitin feels deeply thankful, knowing Chaitanya went out of his way on purpose to help.

qa.q: What could Nitin do with his gratitude now?
qa.a: Thank Chaitanya's mother too, and look out for someone else in need, as Chaitanya did for Nitin.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have said "You'd do it too"?
qa.a: He may have wanted to keep it simple and not make Nitin feel indebted.

grounding: It shows a child recognising and feeling thankful for a friend's deliberate, quiet kindness.

passage: Teacher's note, Uma, Class 4. This morning Rafiq came to me with a card he'd made himself. Yesterday his cycle chain broke on the way to school, and the bus driver, Mani Anna, stopped, put the cycle in the back and brought him in, even though Rafiq doesn't ride that bus. The card said, "Thank you for stopping. You didn't have to." Rafiq asked if he could give it himself. At dismissal he held it out with both hands. I have asked the class to think of one person who helped them on purpose this week.

qa.q: What happened to Rafiq's cycle?
qa.a: Its chain broke on the way to school.

qa.q: What does "You didn't have to" in Rafiq's card show he understood?
qa.a: He understood that Mani Anna chose to help him out of kindness, not because it was his job.

qa.q: Why is Uma's class activity useful?
qa.a: It helps other children notice kindness done on purpose and feel thankful for it.

qa.q: How might Mani Anna feel receiving the card?
qa.a: Touched and appreciated, since a driver's small kindnesses often go unthanked. 🙏

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a boy recognising an adult's intentional kindness and thanking him.

passage:
Dear Diary,
I missed a whole week of school with fever, and I was so scared about the science test. Today Lavanya came to my house with her notebook. She had written all the notes twice, once for her and once for me, in her neat round handwriting, with little drawings of the heart and lungs. She hadn't even told me she was doing it. I almost cried. I tried to give her my best gel pen and she refused, so I'll make her a bookmark instead. I didn't know someone would do that just for me. 🙏
- Swati

qa.q: What had Lavanya drawn in the notes?
qa.a: Little drawings of the heart and lungs.

qa.q: Why did Swati almost cry?
qa.a: Swati was moved that Lavanya had spent time writing notes just for Swati, without being asked or saying a word about it.

qa.q: What is a good way for Swati to show thanks, since Lavanya refused the pen?
qa.a: A handmade bookmark and a sincere thank-you, which match the care Lavanya put in.

qa.q: Why might Lavanya have refused the gel pen?
qa.a: She probably didn't want payment; she helped because she cared, not to get something back.

grounding: It shows a child feeling thankful for a friend's deliberate, unasked-for kindness.

passage: Last month our class made a rule together: no copying homework, even from friends. We all signed the chart. The next week Damini, my bench partner, asked for my maths notebook before the bell. "Just the last sum, please, Tanuja." I said no. She sulked all morning. But when Ma'am checked, and three boys got caught copying, she looked at our row and said, "Thank you for keeping our class promise." My chest felt big and warm. I'd done what we all agreed. Honestly, I felt a bit too pleased with myself when the boys got scolded. Damini talked to me again by lunch.

qa.q: What did the class sign?
qa.a: A chart with the rule of no copying homework.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja's chest feel "big and warm"?
qa.a: Tanuja felt proud and validated for keeping the rule the whole class had agreed on, especially when Ma'am thanked their row.

qa.q: What could Tanuja watch out for about feeling "too pleased" when others got scolded?
qa.a: Keeping a rule is good, but enjoying others' trouble can slide into looking down on them.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt when Tanuja said no?
qa.a: Annoyed and let down at first, which is why she sulked, but she seemed to get over it by lunch.

grounding: It shows a child feeling validated for keeping a rule her class made together, with a hint of smugness.

passage: Games teacher's note, Anjali. In today's inter-house throwball match, the ball touched Uma's fingers before going out, but the umpire gave the point to her team. Uma raised her hand. "Ma'am, it touched me. It's their point." Her team groaned. She stood straight, chin up, and said, "We made the fair-play pledge." They lost by one point. Afterwards she walked around with her head high, telling everyone the pledge mattered more. A few teammates were still sulking. I spoke to the whole team about fair play, and about not lecturing each other.

qa.q: What did Uma tell the umpire?
qa.a: That the ball touched her, so it was the other team's point.

qa.q: What does Uma walking around with her head high after losing suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud and in the right for keeping the fair-play pledge, and that feeling mattered more to her than winning.

qa.q: Why did Anjali also talk about not lecturing each other?
qa.a: Uma's honesty was good, but telling everyone the pledge mattered more could leave teammates feeling judged.

qa.q: How might Uma's teammates feel after losing by one point?
qa.a: Some are upset because her honesty cost them the match, even if they respect the pledge.

grounding: It shows a girl feeling validated by upholding her team's fair-play pledge even at a cost.

passage:
Diary, Saturday.
Clean-up drive in the colony park today. Our Green Club made a rule: whatever you bring, you take back. Karthik threw his chips packet behind the bench. I picked it up, walked over and handed it back to him in front of everyone. "Club rule," I said. He went red and put it in his pocket. The club secretary gave me a thumbs up and said, "Well done, Reena." I felt like a real member, like I was protecting something that belonged to all of us. Maybe I could have said it more quietly, though. Karthik didn't sit with us after.

qa.q: What rule did the Green Club make?
qa.a: Whatever you bring, you take back.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after handing the packet back?
qa.a: Reena felt right and proud, like a true member protecting something shared, though later wondered about the way it was done.

qa.q: What could Reena try next time to uphold the rule without shaming anyone?
qa.a: Remind Karthik quietly or hand him a bag, so he can fix it without an audience.

qa.q: How might Karthik have experienced being corrected in front of everyone?
qa.a: Embarrassed, which may be why he didn't sit with the club afterwards.

grounding: It shows a child feeling validated as a group member by enforcing the club's shared rule.

passage: Nikita, you think I was always good at chess? When I was eleven, I lost every match in the district junior tournament. Seven games, seven losses. I cried behind the hall. My uncle said, "Yusuf, write down every mistake." So I did, in a school notebook. Every evening for a year I replayed my lost games and set up the pieces the way I should have moved. I lost many more times in between. The next year I won four games. Not the trophy, only four. But I remember that feeling better than any trophy since. Keep your notebook, beta.

qa.q: How many games did young Yusuf lose in his first tournament?
qa.a: Seven games, seven losses.

qa.q: What was young Yusuf feeling when he cried behind the hall?
qa.a: Yusuf was crushed and disappointed after losing every match.

qa.q: Why did writing down every mistake help Yusuf?
qa.a: It turned the losses into lessons he could practise, so his effort had a clear direction over the year.

qa.q: Why might Yusuf tell Nikita this story now?
qa.a: Nikita may be facing a setback too, and Yusuf wants Nikita to see that steady effort after losing matters.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, an eleven-year-old recovering from total defeat through a year of steady practice.

passage: Tanuja got 9 out of 30 in the half-yearly science test. That evening the power went off again, and her little cousins were shrieking in the next room. Damini, her older sister, found her on the stairs with the paper crumpled in her lap. "I'm done with science." But after dinner she smoothed the paper out, borrowed Damini's rechargeable lamp and rewrote each wrong answer correctly on a new page. It took three evenings. On the fourth she made a small timetable: twenty minutes of science a day, even with the noise. In the next test she got 17. She stuck both papers on her wall.

qa.q: What did Tanuja get in the half-yearly science test?
qa.a: She got 9 out of 30.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she said "I'm done with science"?
qa.a: Discouraged and hurt after the low score, ready to give up in that moment.

qa.q: Why was a twenty-minute daily timetable a smart choice?
qa.a: Short, steady study was possible even with power cuts and noise, so she could keep going over time.

qa.q: How might Damini see her sister sticking both papers on the wall?
qa.a: As proof of how far Tanuja came by not quitting, which likely makes her proud. 👏

grounding: It shows a girl bouncing back from a poor test score with steady effort despite noise and power cuts.

passage: In the lane behind their building in Lucknow, Anjali, ten, had lost the colony badminton final to Zeenat, 21-8. She went home and didn't come down for two days. On the third evening, Zeenat saw her in the lane at six, alone, hitting the shuttle against the wall. Again. Again. Her backhand kept hitting the gate. She fetched it every time. "Want to practise with me?" Zeenat called. Anjali hesitated, then threw her the spare racquet. "Only if you show me how you did that drop shot." They played until the streetlights came on.

qa.q: What was the score in the final?
qa.a: Zeenat won 21-8.

qa.q: Why might Anjali have stayed home for two days?
qa.a: She was hurt and discouraged after the big loss and needed time before facing the court again.

qa.q: What did Anjali do that helped her bounce back?
qa.a: She returned to steady practice on her own and then asked her rival to teach her the shot that beat her.

qa.q: What might Zeenat feel when Anjali asks about her drop shot?
qa.a: Respected, and glad her friend isn't holding the loss against her.

grounding: It shows a girl returning to practice after losing a final and learning from the person who beat her.

passage: English period note, Rajni. We did riddles today. I asked, "What has hands but can't clap?" Kashish, nine, said, "A clock!" and then added, "And a pair of gloves on a washing line." Later a boy called her "Kashish the Quiz Machine," and she stiffened for a second. Then she saw him grinning, not smirking, and she did a robot voice: "Processing... correct." The class laughed with her. Last term she used to cry at nicknames. Next Friday I will hold a pun hour and talk about teasing that includes versus teasing that hurts.

qa.q: Which riddle did Rajni ask?

passage: At the Tuesday haat in their village, Jagdish Kaka, who sold peanuts, liked to test the children. "Urmila, what goes up but never comes down?" Urmila, ten, frowned at the sky. "A kite? qa.q: Why was Urmila unsure for a moment after the onion comment?

qa.q: What did Urmila's reply show about handling teasing?

passage:
Diary, Monday.
Our class has a book shelf with no lock. Rule: take one, leave one, write your name in the register. Today I saw Minakshi take two comics and leave none. I almost said nothing, since she's my friend. But if everyone did that, the shelf would be empty in a week, and Ma'am trusted us enough not to lock it. So at break I told her quietly. "Sorry, Nilesh," she said. "I forgot to bring one." Tomorrow she'll bring two. I'm glad I said it. It's not about Ma'am catching us. It's about all of us keeping it working.

qa.q: What is the rule for the class book shelf?
qa.a: Take one, leave one, and write your name in the register.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh almost say nothing?
qa.a: Nilesh didn't want to trouble a friend, but also felt the shelf only works if everyone keeps the rule.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's quiet approach get right?
qa.a: Nilesh spoke privately, which let Minakshi fix it without being shamed, and kept the trust-based rule alive.

qa.q: How might Ma'am feel if she heard about this?
qa.a: Pleased that the class is keeping the system fair on its own, showing her trust was well placed.

grounding: It shows a child upholding a shared rule because the system depends on everyone's trust, not on being caught.

passage: At the village hand pump, the rule was simple: one bucket each, then back of the line. Nobody enforced it; it worked because everyone did it. Jasleen, eleven, was fourth in line when her cousin Amandeep ran up. "Let me go before you, just this once. Mummy's shouting." Jasleen looked at the three women behind her, their buckets waiting. "If I let you, they'll let their cousins, and nobody gets water on time." Then she added, "Stand behind me, and I'll help you carry yours after." Amandeep sighed, but got in line.

qa.q: What is the rule at the hand pump?
qa.a: One bucket each, then back of the line.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen look at the women behind her before answering?
qa.a: She was thinking about fairness to them, knowing the line only works if everyone keeps to it.

qa.q: What made Jasleen's answer both fair and kind?
qa.a: She kept the rule but offered to help carry Amandeep's bucket, so he wasn't simply turned away.

qa.q: What would change if Jasleen had let Amandeep skip?
qa.a: Others might start letting their relatives in too, and the trust that keeps the line working could break down.

grounding: It shows a girl keeping a shared queue rule because it rests on everyone's mutual trust.

passage: In their school in Accra, the rule on the veranda was that bags stayed open on the bench during football, and nobody touched anyone else's. qa.q: What did Kofi find beside Nadia's bag?
qa.a: A folded cedi note.

qa.q: Why did Kofi think of the watch Nadia had returned?
qa.a: He felt that trust works both ways, and since she had been honest with him, he wanted to be honest with her.

qa.q: How could Kofi respond if the boys keep saying "finders keepers"?

qa.q: How does Nadia see Kofi returning the money?
qa.a: She is grateful and wants to repay him, showing the give-and-take that keeps their trust going.

grounding: It shows a boy keeping an unwritten rule out of reciprocity and the trust it protects.
